title: The naive framing: "how do I install a plugin for my business?"
text: People think installing a plug-in is the whole job. It isn't. The plug-in arrives generic. So, how do you actually make it customized for your business?

title: Browse by function — the plugin library
text: Open the plug-in section and you'll find a library, an official collection plus community editions. Each listing says what it does and what it covers. Browse by function and find the ones that fit your work. Click install and it

title: Click install — download, activate, ready
text: Downloads, activates, and is ready. No setup wizard. And once it's in, its capabilities just appear. Skills switch on when they're relevant. Slash commands show up in your menu. Connectors sit ready to configure. Nothing to wire up first. A colleague shares a plug-in or

title: Shared plugins upload too
text: You find one from the community, it arrives as a file. Click upload, pick it, and it installs the same way. Same couple of minutes as any other install.

title: You don't do generic — the wrong guess
text: Out of the box, a plug-in runs on sensible defaults, generic best practice for its domain. Useful, but you don't do generic work. You have your own process, your own terms, your own way in.

title: A conversation, not config
text: Click customize and it doesn't open a settings panel, it starts a conversation. It asks about your workflow, your preferences, your tools. You answer in plain language and the plug-in adjusts from what you said. The

title: Ask, answer, calibrate
text: Pattern never changes. It asks, you answer, it calibrates. Ask again, answer again, it tightens. The same loop whether you spend two questions or 20.

title: Your call, your depth
text: How far you take it is your call. Run the defaults, fine, still useful. Or spend a few minutes and get something that feels built for your business. It scales with how central this domain is to your day.

title: The anchor: what does your business do?
text: Say you install a marketing plug-in and click customize. First question, what does your business do and who are your customers? You answer, "A small web design studio. Clients are professional services firms with no marketing team of their own."

title: The studio, and its clients
text: This is the studio the plug-in is about to learn. One person, a few screens, real clients. And these are the clients it now understands. Accountants, lawyers, financial advisers who need a modern site but have no marketing team of their own.

title: Voice, audience, formats — locked in
text: A few more answers, voice is professional but approachable. No jargon, formats are social posts and a monthly newsletter. The plug-in locks it in, the right audience, the right voice, the right formats. Now the output

title: The anchor returns, tuned
text: Changes. Ask for content calendar and you get posts and newsletter topics, not viral video scripts or press releases. A competitive scan targets other web studios, not enterprise agencies. Generic advice becomes advice from someone who knows your business. Some

title: Self-contained or connected
text: Plug-ins are self-contained, useful out of the box, connected to nothing. Others get dramatically more useful the moment you connect them to the tools you already run. A sales plug-in researches

title: Connected reaches further — CRM, live database
text: A prospect from public information alone, decent. Connect it to your CRM and it pulls in your relationship history and every past conversation. Same shape for data. Give it files or connect your live database and it works with your actual numbers directly, no exporting. Connecting is the standard

title: Authorize, then reach
text: Login flow, authorize access the same way you'd link any other app, and it's optional. Start without connections, add them later once you can see the value.

title: Off without erasing
text: Want it to focus? Disable a plug-in without removing it. Your customization stays preserved, waiting. Flip it back on when you need it. Nothing you taught it is lost. Plug-ins improve over time,

title: They keep improving
text: Features get added, issues get fixed, and updates are handled for you. Worth checking in occasionally to see what's new that you might actually use. Loading

title: Two or three, active
text: Up on plug-ins doesn't slow it down or confuse it, but in practice most people keep two or three active. The rest stay installed and disabled, ready the moment a job calls for them.

title: Local to your machine
text: One thing worth knowing, your plug-ins and everything you taught them live on your machine. Work from a second computer and you set them up again there. The customization is personal and it doesn't follow you automatically. After installing, run one test. Type a

title: Test it once
text: Slash to see its commands or just ask it to do the job, build a content calendar for next month, say. A tuned plug-in answers noticeably more structured and aware of your world. Installing a

title: Carry-out
text: Plug-in takes seconds and hands you generic defaults. The conversation afterward about your actual business is what makes it yours.

title: Your turn
text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I just installed a plug-in and I want to customize it for my business instead of running the defaults. Interview me the way the customized conversation would. Ask what my business does and who my customers are. Ask about my voice, my formats, and my terminology. Then summarize the settings you'd apply and show one before and after of how my output changes. Claude

title: Outro
text: Configured installing and customizing plugins. Liam in for bear.
